## Question 22: What GitHub Pages does {#q22}

::: {.stem}
Our static website's repo was already on GitHub. Then we turned on GitHub Pages. What did that do?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} It made the repo private, so that only the class could see the code.

::: {.why}
Wrong. GitHub Pages does not change who can see the repository. A repository is public or private by its own setting; GitHub Pages is free for public repositories.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} It made README.md the website's home page, in place of the main .html file.

::: {.why}
Wrong. README.md is shown on the repository's home page on GitHub, not on the website. The website still starts from its main .html file, often index.html.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[c.]{.letter} It hosted the website online, so that anyone with the link can open it in a browser. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. GitHub Pages is a GitHub feature that hosts a static website. After you turn it on, the site has a public address that anyone can open in a browser.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} It turned the static website into one with logins and stored data.

::: {.why}
Wrong. GitHub Pages serves static files only: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Logins and stored data need a back end, such as a database server, which GitHub Pages does not run.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 12 in Version B (correct answer: a) and question 29 in Version C (correct answer: b). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A **static website** contains only HTML, CSS and JavaScript files. It shows the same content to every visitor. It has no user logins and does not store data. On your own computer, you can open it by double-clicking its main `.html` file (often `index.html`).

Other people cannot open the files on your computer. To put a website on the Internet, the files must be on a **server**: a computer that is always on and runs a **web server program**. This is called **hosting** the website.

Three tools did three different jobs in the class demo:

- **Git** kept the history of the website's files in a **repository** (repo) on your computer.
- **GitHub** stored a copy of the repo online. People can see the code there, and GitHub shows the `README.md` file (from the repo's root folder) on the repo's home page.
- **GitHub Pages** is a GitHub feature that **hosts** a static website from the repo. The site gets an address such as `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repository-name>/`. Anyone with the link can open it in a browser.

The repo on GitHub only shows the code. The GitHub Pages site shows the working website.

After you set it up, every push of new commits to GitHub updates the live site after a minute or two. This is called **push to deploy**.

GitHub Pages hosts static files only. A website with logins and stored data (a **dynamic** website) needs server-side code and a database. The course's task app used other services for that: Vercel to host the web server and Supabase for the database and logins.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 40 Hosting and Deployment: Getting Your App Online › Deploying from GitHub](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/040700-hostingAndDeployment-v001.html#deploying-from-github)
- [Ch. 31 Putting Your Repository on GitHub › README.md and Markdown](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/030600-githubRemotes-v001.html#readme.md-and-markdown)
- [Ch. 36 What Happens on the Server: Back Ends, Databases, and APIs › Static vs. dynamic websites](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/040400-whatHappensOnTheServer-v001.html#static-vs.-dynamic-websites)

## Question 23: Risk of a powerful AI's goal {#q23}

::: {.stem}
Why is it risky to give a very powerful AI a goal such as "Make as much money for me as possible," even if the AI is not "evil"?
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[a.]{.letter} The AI may reach the goal in harmful ways that the person never intended. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. A very powerful AI may find a way to reach the goal that harms people, although the person never intended or expected it. The AI does not need to be "evil"; people are just in the way of its goal.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} The AI can't know today's stock prices, because of its training cutoff.

::: {.why}
Wrong. A model's training data does stop at its knowledge cutoff, but an agent can use tools such as web search to get current prices. Also, a lack of data is a limit, not the danger that the question asks about.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} The AI will keep the money for itself, instead of giving it to the person.

::: {.why}
Wrong. This choice assumes that the AI wants money for itself. The risk in question does not need an AI with its own selfish plans; it comes from an AI that does exactly what it was asked, by any means.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} The AI will refuse, because money goals break its safety rules.

::: {.why}
Wrong. A goal to make money is not against safety rules in general; it is a normal request. The risk is not that the AI refuses, but that it reaches the goal in harmful ways.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} The AI will use so many tokens that the cost is more than the profit.

::: {.why}
Wrong. An agent can spend more on tokens than it earns, so this can happen. But it will not always happen, and it is not the risk that the question asks about: harm that the person never intended.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 37 in Version B (correct answer: d) and question 38 in Version C (correct answer: d). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Alignment** means that an AI uses its abilities the way people intend. **Misalignment** means that it pursues goals that conflict with those intentions.

A common idea from films is an AI that is "evil" and hates people. The risk discussed in class is different. A very powerful AI that only tries to reach its goal can harm people because people are in the way, not because it is against them.

The class example: a person tells an AI, "Make as much money for me on the stock market as possible." The AI finds this plan: hack into Waymo's self-driving cars, short Waymo's stock (bet that its price will fall), make the cars crash, and collect the profit. The person never intended this and never thought the AI would do it. The AI only tried to reach its goal.

A comparison from class: people who pave a road do not hate the ants in its path. They just do not think about the ants. A powerful AI could treat people the same way.

The **paper clip** example makes the same point: an AI whose only goal is to make paper clips could use every resource it can reach for paper clips, with no thought for people.

The lesson: a goal such as "as much as possible" has no limits. A person assumes many limits (obey the law, harm nobody) without saying them. A powerful AI does not automatically know or follow limits that nobody stated. The more capable the AI, the more ways it can find to reach a goal, including harmful ways.

- [Ch. 2 What Is AI Safety? › Three kinds of risk](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/005100-whatIsAiSafety-v001.html#three-kinds-of-risk)

## Question 24: Input tokens and output tokens {#q24}

::: {.stem}
You send Claude a question that is 1,000 tokens long, and it replies with 1,000 tokens. Which is generally true about the cost?
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[a.]{.letter} The reply costs more, because output tokens are generally more expensive. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. You pay for input tokens and for output tokens, and output tokens generally cost more. With the same number of each, the reply costs more.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} The question costs more, because input tokens are generally more expensive.

::: {.why}
Wrong. This choice swaps the two prices. Input tokens (what you send) are generally cheaper than output tokens (what the model replies).
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Only the reply costs anything, because input tokens are always free.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Input tokens are not free. You pay for the tokens you send and for the tokens the model replies.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} The cost depends on the number of messages, not on the tokens.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Charges come from the number of tokens, not the number of messages. A long message costs more than a short one.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} Both cost the same, because every token has the same price.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Tokens do not all have the same price. Output tokens are generally more expensive than input tokens, and prices also differ from model to model.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 11 in Version B (correct answer: a) and question 36 in Version C (correct answer: a). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A **token** is a common sequence of characters, such as a short word or part of a longer word. Models read and write text as tokens, and the cost of using a model is counted in tokens.

There are two kinds:

- **Input tokens**: the tokens in the text that you *send* to the model.
- **Output tokens**: the tokens in the text that the model *replies* to you. The model's thinking tokens are billed like output tokens.

Output tokens are generally more expensive than input tokens. For example, in the course's October 2026 price list, Opus 5.5 cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Output cost five times as much as input for every Claude model in that list.

There are two ways to pay:

- With the **API** ("pay as you go"), you pay for each token that you use.
- With a **subscription** (such as Pro or Max), you pay a fixed monthly price. Your plan's usage limits are still based on how many tokens you use. When you reach a limit, you wait until it resets.

Input tokens add up quickly in a long conversation. With every new message, Claude Code sends the whole conversation again. The part that the server already processed is cached, which makes it much cheaper to read again, but it is still input. This is one reason to keep conversations short with `/clear`, `/compact` and `/rewind`.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 43 Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits › Two ways to pay: subscription or API](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/050200-claudeModelsPlansAndUsage-v001.html#two-ways-to-pay-subscription-or-api)
- [Ch. 43 Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits › Plans and prices (a dated snapshot)](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/050200-claudeModelsPlansAndUsage-v001.html#plans-and-prices-a-dated-snapshot)
- [Ch. 8 How Large Language Models Work › Tokens](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010200-howLlmsWork-v001.html#tokens)

## Question 25: Private data and local models {#q25}

::: {.stem}
A hospital wants AI to summarize patient records, but it must not send the records to an outside company. Which choice is best, and what is the tradeoff?
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[a.]{.letter} Run a local model; the data stays inside, but the model is less capable. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. A local model runs on the hospital's own computers, so the records never go to an outside company. The tradeoff is that a local model is slower and less capable than a frontier model.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} Run a frontier model on a staff laptop; it is just as good, and free.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Frontier models need very expensive hardware, far more than a laptop has. A laptop can run only much smaller models, and those are less capable.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Use an online frontier model but tell them not to read the data.

::: {.why}
Wrong. With an online model, the records still go to the outside company. A request not to read them does not change that, and it breaks the hospital's rule.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} Use a frontier online model but encrypt your data before sending it to them.

::: {.why}
Wrong. The model must be able to read the records to summarize them, so the company must receive them in a form it can read. The records still go to the outside company.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 38 in Version B (correct answer: b) and question 37 in Version C (correct answer: b). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

There are two ways to run an AI model.

A **hosted** (cloud) model runs on the AI company's computers. You use it through the company's app or API. Every prompt you send, including any data in it, goes to that company.

A **local** model runs on your own hardware. Your data stays on your machines.

| | Hosted (cloud) model | Local model |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | The provider's data centers | Your own computers |
| Your data | Sent to the provider | Stays with you |
| Capability | The most capable models | Smaller models: useful, but usually behind |
| Speed | Fast | Slower |
| Setup | None | You install and update everything |

**Frontier models** are the most capable models. They are very expensive to train and to run. They need hardware far beyond what a person can run at home. Much smaller models can run on a laptop. Larger organizations can run bigger models on their own servers, but these are still usually behind the frontier.

To run a model locally, you need its trained **weights**. An **open-weight** model is one whose weights are published, so anyone can download it and run it. Free apps such as Ollama and LM Studio do this.

A local model is the right choice when privacy matters: patient data, student data, financial data, or a company's private data. The tradeoff is clear: you keep control of the data, but you accept a slower and less capable model.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 9 Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use › Local models vs. cloud models](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010300-limitsRisksAndResponsibleUse-v001.html#local-models-vs.-cloud-models)
- [Ch. 7 What AI Can Do Today › Open-weight vs. closed models](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010100-whatAiCanDoToday-v001.html#open-weight-vs.-closed-models)

## Question 26: How a tokenizer splits text {#q26}

::: {.stem}
A tokenizer splits the text "Elephants are enormous." into tokens. Which is correct?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} The whole sentence becomes one token, because it is short.

::: {.why}
Wrong. A short sentence is not one token. Tokens are common sequences of characters from the training data, and a whole sentence is far too rare to be one token.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} Each letter becomes its own token, including the spaces.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Most tokens are longer than one letter. Some tokens are a single letter or symbol, but a tokenizer uses longer tokens wherever it can.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Each word becomes exactly one token, no matter how long it is.

::: {.why}
Wrong. A word does not always become one token. A common word is often one token, but a long or rare word is split into several pieces.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[d.]{.letter} Some words become one token, others become several tokens. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. A short, common word such as "are" is likely to be one token. A longer or rarer word can be split into several tokens. The exact split depends on the tokenizer.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} All models share the same tokens, so every model splits it the same way.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Different models can use different tokenizers and different sets of tokens. The same text can become different tokens, and a different number of tokens, on different models.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 43 in Version B (correct answer: e) and question 20 in Version C (correct answer: e). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

LLMs do not read letters or whole words. Before a model sees your text, a program called a **tokenizer** splits the text into **tokens**.

A **token** is a sequence of characters that occurs often in the training data. Characters include letters, spaces, digits and punctuation. So:

- A common word is often one token.
- A longer or rarer word is split into several tokens. For example, "dictionary" might be three tokens: `dict-ion-ary`.
- Some tokens are part of a word, such as `'s`. Some tokens are a single letter or symbol.
- Spaces and punctuation count too.

For example, a tokenizer might split "Dinosaurs were dangerous!" like this (dashes show where one token ends and the next starts): `Dino-saur-s- -we-re- d-anger-ous-!`

Each model has a fixed set of tokens, called its **vocabulary**. Different models can use different vocabularies. Frontier models today can have about 200,000 tokens in their vocabulary; smaller models might have about 50,000. So the same text can become a different number of tokens on different models.

Tokens matter because:

- An LLM generates the next **token**, not the next word.
- **Prices** and **limits** (such as the size of the context window) are counted in tokens.
- Some tasks that are easy for people, such as counting letters in a word, are hard for a model that sees tokens instead of letters.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 8 How Large Language Models Work › Tokens](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010200-howLlmsWork-v001.html#tokens)
- [Ch. 8 How Large Language Models Work › An LLM predicts the next token](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010200-howLlmsWork-v001.html#an-llm-predicts-the-next-token)

## Question 27: Client and server roles {#q27}

::: {.stem}
A browser asks a web server for a page. To build the page, the web server program asks the database server for data. In that second request, what role does the web server play?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} A database, because it stores the data itself.

::: {.why}
Wrong. The web server program does not store the app's data. The database server stores the data and provides it when asked.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} None, because the browser asks the database directly.

::: {.why}
Wrong. In this setup, the browser asks the web server, and the web server asks the database server. The browser does not talk to the database directly.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} A server, because a web server only provides data and never requests it.

::: {.why}
Wrong. A program can be a server in one request and a client in another. The web server program provides pages to the browser, but it requests data from the database server.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[d.]{.letter} A client, because it requests data from the database server. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. A client is the program that requests data. In the second request, the web server program asks the database server for data, so it is a client of the database server.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} A browser, because it shows the data to the user.

::: {.why}
Wrong. The web server program does not show anything to the user. The browser shows the page; the web server program only sends it.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 8 in Version B (correct answer: b) and question 8 in Version C (correct answer: a). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The words **client** and **server** describe roles in a request:

- A **client** is a program that *requests* data.
- A **server** is a program that *provides* data.

"Server" can also mean the computer that runs a server program; the context tells you which.

A web application usually has three programs:

1. The **browser** (Chrome, Safari, ...) is a client. It asks the web server for a page.
2. The **web server program** sends HTML, CSS and JavaScript to the browser. To build a page, it often needs data, so it asks the database server for it, in the **SQL** language.
3. The **database server program** (for example PostgreSQL) stores the data and provides it.

```
browser  --request-->  web server program  --SQL request-->  database server program
(client)               (server, then client)                  (server)
```

So one program can have two roles. The web server program is a **server** to the browser and a **client** of the database server. The role depends on which request you look at.

All three programs can run on one computer, or on different computers. For example, while you develop an app, the web server can run on your own computer at `localhost:3000`.

The same idea applies in the course's task app. Supabase is a server to the browser. The Edge Functions on Supabase are in turn clients of OpenAI and Stripe.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 33 Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP › Clients and servers](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/040100-browsersAndWebServers-v001.html#clients-and-servers)
- [Ch. 36 What Happens on the Server: Back Ends, Databases, and APIs › Databases](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/040400-whatHappensOnTheServer-v001.html#databases)
- [Ch. 71 Project Architecture › Project Architecture](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/001007-tutorial-supabase-projectArchitecture-v001.html#project-architecture)

## Question 28: /compact and /clear {#q28}

::: {.stem}
What is the difference between `/compact` and `/clear` in Claude Code?
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[a.]{.letter} `/compact` keeps a summary of the conversation; `/clear` starts a new chat without one. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. /compact replaces the conversation with a summary, so you can continue the same task with more free space. /clear erases the conversation and starts a new chat with no summary.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} They do the same thing; `/compact` is just an older name for `/clear`.

::: {.why}
Wrong. They do different things. /compact keeps a summary of the conversation; /clear keeps nothing from the conversation.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Both erase the whole conversation; `/compact` also removes CLAUDE.md from the context.

::: {.why}
Wrong. /compact does not erase the whole conversation; it keeps a summary. Neither command removes CLAUDE.md: Claude Code loads it again after both.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} `/compact` makes your project's files smaller; `/clear` deletes them from your computer.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Both commands change only the conversation in the context window. Neither command changes or deletes the files on your computer.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} `/clear` keeps a summary of the conversation; `/compact` starts a new chat without one.

::: {.why}
Wrong. This choice swaps the two commands. /compact is the one that keeps a summary; /clear starts a new chat without one.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 16 in Version B (correct answer: a) and question 21 in Version C (correct answer: b). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The **context window** is the model's working memory: the maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that it can consider at once. It holds the **system prompt**, your CLAUDE.md files, the skill descriptions, the conversation, files Claude read, and tool results.

A full context window causes problems:

- **Context rot**: as the window fills, the model starts to forget things, especially from the middle of the conversation.
- **Cost**: Claude Code sends the whole conversation again with every message, so a long conversation uses more tokens.

Claude Code has commands to keep the used part of the window small:

| Command | What it does | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `/compact` | Replaces the conversation with a summary | You want to continue the same task |
| `/compact pay special attention to ...` | The same, but tells the summary what to keep | You know what matters next |
| `/clear` | Erases the conversation and starts a new chat | You switch to an unrelated task |
| `/rewind` | Goes back to an earlier prompt in the conversation | A path went wrong |

After `/clear`, CLAUDE.md, the system prompt and the skill descriptions are still loaded. Only the conversation is gone. Claude Code also compacts by itself when the window is nearly full.

A summary can lose details. That is why rules that must last belong in CLAUDE.md, not only in the chat.

None of these commands changes your project's files. They change only what is in the context window.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 52 Context, Models, Effort, and Usage › Freeing up context: /compact, /clear, and friends](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/060800-contextModelsEffortAndUsage-v001.html#freeing-up-context-compact-clear-and-friends)
- [Ch. 52 Context, Models, Effort, and Usage › The context window in practice](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/060800-contextModelsEffortAndUsage-v001.html#the-context-window-in-practice)
- [Ch. 48 Essential Slash Commands (the whole chapter)](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/060400-slashCommands-v001.html)

## Question 29: Temperature and predictable answers {#q29}

::: {.stem}
A bank wants its AI to stick closely to the most probable words, so that its answers are predictable. A novelist wants the AI to pick less likely words more often, so that its writing is surprising. Which setting controls this?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} The effort level

::: {.why}
Wrong. The effort level sets how much the model thinks before it answers. It does not control how often the model picks less likely words.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} The number of tokens in the model's vocabulary

::: {.why}
Wrong. The vocabulary is the fixed set of tokens that a model uses. It does not decide how strictly the model picks from them.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} The size of the context window

::: {.why}
Wrong. The context window is how much text the model can consider at once. It does not change how the model picks the next word.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} The number of parameters in the model

::: {.why}
Wrong. The number of parameters measures the size of the model. It is fixed by training and is not a setting for how predictable the answers are.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[e.]{.letter} The temperature [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. Temperature sets how strictly the model sticks to the most probable words. A low temperature suits the bank; a higher temperature suits the novelist.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 36 in Version B (correct answer: c) and question 31 in Version C (correct answer: d). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

For each next word (more exactly, each next **token**), a model calculates a **probability distribution**: a probability for every token it knows. For "The boy went to the ___", "store" and "school" have high probabilities, and "purple" has a very low one. The software then picks one token from this distribution. It usually picks a likely token, but not always the most likely one. With two dice, 7 is the most likely total, but other totals also happen.

**Temperature** is the setting that controls how this pick is made. It is typically a number between 0 and 1.

- **Low temperature** (near 0): the model almost always picks the most probable token. Answers are more predictable. At 0, it always picks the most probable token, although the output is still not guaranteed to be identical every time.
- **Higher temperature** (near 1): the model picks according to the learned probabilities, so less likely tokens are picked more often. Answers are more varied and surprising, but also more likely to go off track.

Do not confuse temperature with other settings and sizes:

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| Effort | How much the model thinks before it answers |
| Context window | How much text the model can consider at once |
| Vocabulary | The set of tokens the model uses |
| Parameters | The model's weights; their number measures the model's size |

Chat apps choose the temperature for you. Many developer APIs let you set it, but some newer models, including Anthropic's newest Claude models, no longer allow you to change it.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 8 How Large Language Models Work › Choosing the next token](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010200-howLlmsWork-v001.html#choosing-the-next-token)
- [Ch. 8 How Large Language Models Work › An LLM predicts the next token](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010200-howLlmsWork-v001.html#an-llm-predicts-the-next-token)

## Question 30: Where to put a standing rule {#q30}

::: {.stem}
You want Claude Code to follow a rule every time it works on your project: "Run the tests before you say that a task is done." Where should this rule go?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} In README.md

::: {.why}
Wrong. README.md describes the repository for people, and GitHub shows it on the repository's home page. Claude Code does not load it automatically as a set of rules.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} In a skill

::: {.why}
Wrong. Claude Code loads a skill's full instructions only when it decides that they are useful, or when you type the skill's slash command. A rule that must apply every time could be missed.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[c.]{.letter} In CLAUDE.md [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md automatically at the start of every session in that folder. Claude sees the rule every time it works on the project.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} In the system prompt

::: {.why}
Wrong. The system prompt is written by the maker of the tool, not by you. You cannot put your own project's rules there.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} In an MCP server

::: {.why}
Wrong. An MCP server connects Claude to an outside service and gives it new tools. It is not a place for rules about how Claude works.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 41 in Version B (correct answer: d) and question 9 in Version C (correct answer: b). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Each Claude Code session starts with a fresh **context window**, Claude's working memory. Claude does not remember earlier sessions by itself. **CLAUDE.md** is a plain-text Markdown file that gives Claude standing instructions: how to run the project, the team's rules, mistakes to avoid.

How CLAUDE.md works:

- Claude Code puts CLAUDE.md into the context automatically, at the start of **every session** in that folder.
- You can have different CLAUDE.md files in different folders. A project's CLAUDE.md is usually committed to Git, so the whole team shares it.
- After `/clear` or `/compact`, CLAUDE.md is still loaded.
- **AGENTS.md** does the same job. It became the standard file name for all AI coding tools, and Claude Code also recognizes it.

Compare CLAUDE.md with a **skill**. Only a skill's description is always in the context; its full instructions load only when Claude decides they are useful. So:

| Kind of instruction | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| A rule for all work on the project ("run the tests before you say a task is done") | `CLAUDE.md` |
| A procedure for one kind of task ("make the weekly sales report") | A skill |

Keep CLAUDE.md short. Everything in it uses context space in every session.

One more fact: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not a guarantee. Claude reads it and tries to follow it, but nothing forces it to. If something must never happen, use a permission rule or a hook instead.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 50 CLAUDE.md and Memory › Why Claude needs a memory file](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/060600-claudeMdAndMemory-v001.html#why-claude-needs-a-memory-file)
- [Ch. 50 CLAUDE.md and Memory › Where CLAUDE.md files live](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/060600-claudeMdAndMemory-v001.html#where-claude.md-files-live)
- [Ch. 55 Extending Claude Code: The Big Picture › The extension points at a glance](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/070100-extendingOverview-v001.html#the-extension-points-at-a-glance)

## Question 31: What a static website can do {#q31}

::: {.stem}
Which of these could be built as a **static website** (only HTML, CSS and JavaScript files)?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} A site where visitors post comments that later visitors can read.

::: {.why}
Wrong. The site must save each comment and show it to later visitors. That needs a database and server-side code, and a static website has neither.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[b.]{.letter} A restaurant's site that shows its menu, hours and address, the same for every visitor. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. The menu, hours and address are the same for every visitor. Only the owner changes them, by editing the files, so HTML, CSS and JavaScript files are enough.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} A site where visitors create accounts and log in to see their saved favorites.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Accounts and logins need a way to know who is asking, and saved favorites need data storage for each user. A static website has no users, no logins and no data storage.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} A site that recommends products based on what each visitor bought before.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Recommendations based on past purchases need a stored record of what each visitor bought. A static website cannot store data or tell one visitor from another.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 13 in Version B (correct answer: a) and question 43 in Version C (correct answer: a). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A **static website** is a set of files that were prepared ahead of time: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The web server sends the same files to every visitor. You can even open a static website on your own computer by double-clicking its main `.html` file. The olympics demo site from class and this book are static websites.

On a static website:

- every visitor sees the same information;
- only the owner changes what the site shows, by changing the files;
- there are no users and no logins;
- nothing that a visitor does is stored.

A **dynamic website** runs code on the server for each request. That code builds a page for *that* user at *that* moment, for example your order history or your bank balance. A dynamic website needs three things that a static website does not have:

- **server-side code** (code that runs on the server, not in the browser);
- a **database** (a program that stores data and gives it back when asked);
- a way to know **who is asking** (logging in).

A static website can still be interactive. JavaScript can open menus or show photos when you click, because this happens in your browser and nothing is saved.

To decide if a site can be static, ask two questions. Does the site need to remember something that a visitor did? Does it show different content to different visitors? If the answer to both is no, a static website is enough.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 36 What Happens on the Server: Back Ends, Databases, and APIs › Static vs. dynamic websites](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/040400-whatHappensOnTheServer-v001.html#static-vs.-dynamic-websites)
- [Ch. 36 What Happens on the Server: Back Ends, Databases, and APIs › Databases](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/040400-whatHappensOnTheServer-v001.html#databases)

## Question 32: Agentic AI tools vs. coding tools {#q32}

::: {.stem}
Which task is the best fit for an agentic AI tool, such as Muse, and not for Claude Code?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} Write a program that adds two 100-digit numbers exactly.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Exact arithmetic with big numbers is a programming job. A coding tool such as Claude Code can write and run a short program that adds the numbers exactly.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} Turn a folder of code into a git repo and put it on GitHub.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Creating a git repo and uploading it to GitHub is software-development work. In class, Claude Code did exactly this for the demo website.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Find the bug that makes your app crash when a user logs in.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Finding a bug in an app's code is a core job of a coding tool. Claude Code can read the code, run it and change it.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[d.]{.letter} Each morning, answer meeting requests in your email and reorder office supplies. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. Answering email and ordering supplies are everyday tasks, not software work. Agentic AI tools focus on getting such things done, and they can do almost anything online that a person can.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[e.]{.letter} Build a website for your club out of HTML, CSS and JavaScript files.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Building a website from HTML, CSS and JavaScript files is software development. In class, Claude Code built a static website in this way.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 14 in Version B (correct answer: a) and question 4 in Version C (correct answer: b). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Generative AI** makes content: a chat tool writes text, and other tools make images, music or video. **Agentic AI** *does* things with tools. It can change files on your computer, run programs, browse the web, search for information and place orders.

The course sorts AI tools into three groups:

| Group | Main focus | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Chat tools | Conversation in a web page or app | ChatGPT, claude.ai, Grok |
| Coding tools | Building software | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor |
| Agentic AI tools | Getting everyday things done | Open Claw, Hermes, Muse (Meta), Dots (OpenAI), Grokbot (xAI) |

Coding tools are agentic too. Claude Code reads and edits files and runs commands on your computer. But its focus is software: writing programs, fixing bugs, using git and GitHub, and building websites.

Agentic AI tools focus on everyday tasks. They can do almost anything online that a person can, such as answering email, booking meetings or ordering products. They can also change files and run programs.

The groups change over time. For example, the claude.ai web interface now has some Claude Code features. To pick the best tool, look at the goal of the task. If the result is software, a coding tool is the best fit. If the result is an everyday job done for you, an agentic AI tool is the best fit.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 11 AI-Assisted Development: From Chatbots to Coding Agents › What makes a tool an agent](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010400-aiAssistedDevelopment-v001.html#what-makes-a-tool-an-agent)
- [Ch. 12 The AI Coding Tool Landscape (Fall 2026) › Categories of AI coding tools](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010500-aiCodingToolsLandscape-v001.html#categories-of-ai-coding-tools)
- [Ch. 7 What AI Can Do Today › Acting in the world](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/010100-whatAiCanDoToday-v001.html#acting-in-the-world)

## Question 33: Bash on Mac, Linux and Windows {#q33}

::: {.stem}
A Mac user, a Linux user and a Windows user all want to use the Bash commands that we learned in class. Which is correct?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} Windows already has Bash built in; it is called CMD.

::: {.why}
Wrong. CMD is the original command-line language of Windows, not Bash. It can do the same jobs as Bash, but with different commands.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[b.]{.letter} The Mac and Linux users have Bash; the Windows user can install it, for example with Git Bash. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. Bash is available on Mac and Linux. Windows does not include it, but you can install it for free, for example with Git Bash, which we used in class.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Only the Linux user has Bash; Macs and Windows use PowerShell instead.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Macs have Bash too, so a Mac user can use the same commands as a Linux user. PowerShell comes with Windows; the Mac comes with Bash.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} None of them has Bash until they install it, because no operating system includes it.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Mac and Linux already include Bash. Only the Windows user must install it.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 3 in Version B (correct answer: d) and question 11 in Version C (correct answer: d). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A **CLI** (command-line interface) lets you control the computer by typing commands in a **terminal** program. The program that reads and runs your commands is the **shell**. Each shell has its own command language.

**Bash** is probably the most popular command language. The commands we learned in class, such as `pwd`, `ls`, `cd` and `mv`, are Bash commands.

| Computer | Bash? | Other command languages |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | Included | |
| Mac | Included | zsh, the Mac's default shell; for the class commands it works the same as Bash |
| Windows | Not included; install it, for example with **Git Bash** (free) or WSL2 | **PowerShell** (newer, more powerful) and **CMD** (the original, simpler) |

Bash, PowerShell and CMD can all do the same jobs, such as moving files or making folders. They use different commands to do them. So a Bash command that you learned in class does not always work in PowerShell or CMD.

In this course, Windows users installed Git Bash. After that, all three users can type the same Bash commands and get the same results. (We did not cover WSL2.)

## Question 34: GitHub's role in team projects {#q34}

::: {.stem}
Three students work together on the same project. What role does GitHub play?
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[a.]{.letter} Each student clones the repo and shares changes with the others through it. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. GitHub keeps a copy of the repo online. Each student clones it to download a copy, uploads their own changes to GitHub, and downloads the changes that the others made.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} GitHub emails each student a new copy of the code whenever someone saves a file.

::: {.why}
Wrong. GitHub does not email copies of code, and saving a file does not send anything. Each student downloads the others' changes from GitHub when they choose.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} Only the repo's owner can download it; the others email their changes to the owner.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Other people can clone a repo too: anyone can clone a public repo, and the people that the owner allows can clone a private repo. Team members share changes through GitHub, not by email.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} GitHub replaces git, so the students don't need git on their computers.

::: {.why}
Wrong. GitHub is a website for git repos; it does not replace git. Each student still uses git on their own computer to record changes and to send them to GitHub.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 4 in Version B (correct answer: c) and question 42 in Version C (correct answer: d). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Git** is a program that runs on your computer. It records versions of the files in a project folder. A folder that git tracks is a **repository** (**repo**). Git works offline and needs no account.

**GitHub** is a website that stores copies of git repos on the Internet. It is not the same as git. You need an account and an Internet connection to use it.

How a team works with GitHub:

1. One person uploads the repo to GitHub.
2. Each team member **clones** the repo. Cloning downloads a copy of the repo, with its whole history, to your computer. The copy remembers where it came from.
3. Each person changes files and records the changes with git on their own computer.
4. Each person uploads (**pushes**) their changes to GitHub and downloads (**pulls**) the changes that the others made.

To coordinate the work of many people on one repo, you need more git ideas, which the course covers later.

A GitHub repo can be **public** (anyone can see it) or **private** (only you and the people you allow can see it). GitHub is also useful for one person: you get an online copy of your work that you can use from anywhere, and you can show your work to others.

**Read more in the course book:**

- [Ch. 26 What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub) › Git vs. GitHub](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/030100-whatIsVersionControl-v001.html#git-vs.-github)
- [Ch. 32 Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers) (the whole chapter)](https://y-rosenthal.github.io/aiasd-in-progress/030700-cloneAndPull-v001.html)

## Question 35: Vercel's job in the task app {#q35}

::: {.stem}
What is Vercel's job in the task app's architecture?
:::

::: {.choice}
[a.]{.letter} It sends each new task to an AI model and gets back a label.

::: {.why}
Wrong. This is the job of the OpenAI API. An Edge Function on Supabase sends the new task to OpenAI and gets back the label.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[b.]{.letter} It checks users' passwords and handles "Sign in with Google".

::: {.why}
Wrong. Supabase does authentication, including "Sign in with Google" (with Google's sign-in service). Vercel does not check passwords.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[c.]{.letter} It stores the app's data, such as each user's tasks and profile.

::: {.why}
Wrong. Supabase stores the app's data, in its PostgreSQL database.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
[d.]{.letter} It stores the app's code and keeps the history of every change.

::: {.why}
Wrong. GitHub stores the code and the history of every change; your copy is a fork. Vercel imports the code from GitHub, but it is not where the code and its history are kept.
:::
:::

::: {.choice .correct}
[e.]{.letter} It hosts the website online, so anyone can open the app at a public address. [(correct answer)]{.correct-tag}

::: {.why}
Correct. Once the app is online, Vercel is the web server. It imports the code from GitHub, builds the app and hosts it at a public address, so anyone can open it.
:::
:::

[In the other versions, this was question 30 in Version B (correct answer: c) and question 19 in Version C (correct answer: e). The choices are in a different order in each version.]{.other-versions}

### Background {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A **web server** is a program that sends a website's pages to browsers. A **host** is a company whose computers run your website on the Internet.

The task app runs in two places at different times:

- **While you develop**, the web server is a **development server** on your own computer. Its address is `localhost:3000`, which means "the program on this computer that listens on port 3000". Nobody else can open it.
- **After you deploy**, the same app runs on **Vercel** at a public address. Anyone with the address can open it.

In both places, the back end is the same Supabase project.

**Deploying** means putting the app online. With Vercel it works like this:

1. Vercel imports your repository (your fork) from GitHub.
2. Vercel builds the app and hosts it at a public address.
3. From then on, every push to your fork makes Vercel deploy the new version automatically.

You give Vercel only the Supabase URL and the publishable key. You give it no secret keys, because the secrets stay on Supabase.

Each part of the tech stack has one job. Vercel hosts the website. Supabase gives the database, logins, image storage and Edge Functions. GitHub stores the code. Google, OpenAI and Stripe do sign-in, AI labels and payments.
